The Turbine software can simulate network dynamics on very large networks (millions of nodes and edges) on a standard desktop computer.
The 'communicating vessels' model used in Turbine gives an exponential decay of perturbations, in agreement with several earlier findings.
Benchmark graphs with pronounced modular structure trapped high-intensity perturbations within their modules, while those with fuzzy modules did not show this 'module encapsulation' effect.
Perturbation centrality is defined as the reciprocal of the 'silencing time', which is the first time when all nodes have an energy value less than a pre-set threshold after an initial perturbation.
Perturbation centrality was highly correlated with closeness centrality (r=0.67), community centrality (r=0.65), and weighted degree (r=0.69) across various networks.
In networks with pronounced modules, inter-modular non-hubs had 87% larger perturbation centrality than intra-modular hubs on average.
Perturbation centrality correctly identified amino acids involved in intra-protein communication and substrate binding sites in the Met-tRNA synthetase protein structure network.

Changes in perturbation centralities of yeast interactome nodes recapitulated the functional changes of stressed yeast cells, with heat-shocked cells showing a 40.5% lower average perturbation centrality compared to unstressed cells.
